newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin bids to end Kremlin feud by sacking Lebed.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin bids to end Kremlin feud by sacking Lebed.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin tried to crush a Kremlin power struggle on Thursday by sacking security tsar Alexander Lebed, saying he could no longer tolerate his lack of team spirit and ambition to become Russia's next leader.

Yeltsin's dramatic move could end months of worsening squabbles between Lebed and his rivals but leaves a huge question mark over a fragile peace accord negotiated by Lebed in Chechnya, which has met strong opposition in Moscow.

Yeltsin might also have made a rod for his own back, since a recent opinion poll showed the outspoken former paratroop general was the most trusted politician in Russia and thus a possible focus for the opposition.

The Russian leader's patience was clearly at an end when he went on television to castigate Lebed for his failings and then signed a decree dismissing him from his twin posts as national security adviser and secretary of the powerful Security Council.
"I can no longer tolerate this situation and I am forced to relieve General Lebed of his position as secretary of the Security Council," announced Yeltsin, who looked stiff but spoke with feeling.
Lebed has been drawn into an increasingly bitter power struggle with other Kremlin officials since Yeltsin said on September 5 he was preparing to undergo heart surgery.
The outspoken general, in what appeared to be his first comments after the sacking, told Ekho Moskvy radio: "I am not worried...I've never begged and will never beg."

The final straw for Yeltsin seems to have been an extraordinary clash on Wednesday between Lebed and Interior Minister Anatoly Kulikov, just one day after the Russian leader told his Kremlin team to stop squabbling.

Kulikov -- who accused his rival of preparing to use force to seize power -- is one of the fiercest opponents of the August 31 peace deal which Lebed signed with separatist Chechen leaders to end a bloody 21-month war.
Asked whether he expected events in Chechnya to go according to "the worst possible scenario" after his dismissal, Lebed answered: "In all probability, yes".
In the Chechen capital Grozny, rebel leaders had earlier predicted the war would flare up again if Lebed went.
"If they get rid of Lebed we will have to prepare for war because you can expect anything from people like Kulikov," rebel chief-of-staff Aslan Maskhadov told Reuters.

Yeltsin appointed Lebed to his posts in mid-June in a successful bid to fend off the threat from communist challenger Gennady Zyuganov in the second round of presidential elections but Lebed's lack of guile meant he soon started making enemies.
The communists were quick to gloat over the sacking, saying they had pointed out from the start that Yeltsin only appointed Lebed in a last-ditch bid to defeat Zyuganov.
"The Moor has done his duty, let him go," said Communist Party secretary Viktor Zorkaltsev, quoting from Shakespeare's play Othello.
Before the sacking, Zyuganov said the row "could end in a general civil war as well as destroying the army".

From the start it became clear that Lebed was ill-versed in the subtle art of political infighting. In August he held a news conference to demand Yeltsin choose between him and Kulikov, but the Russian leader merely told him to shut up and knuckle down.
"There has to be a united team; the team should pull together, work like a fist," Yeltsin said on Thursday.
"But now we have a situation whereby Lebed is splitting the team apart and is carrying out a number of moves which he did not agree with the president. This is totally unacceptable."
Lebed, who came a strong third in the first round of the presidential polls in June, has made no secret of his desire to lead the country.

"The election won't be held until the year 2000 and already we have a situation where everyone seems to want to take part in an election. Of course, such a situation can no longer be tolerated," complained Yeltsin.
Earlier on Thursday Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin appealed to the military to stay calm.

Authorities in Moscow and other Russian cities have stepped up security after the allegations by Kulikov, who also said 1,500 Chechen gunmen would help Lebed seize power. Both Lebed and Maskhadov denied the allegations.
